title: Estimation and Rounding of Large Numbers
seo_title: Estimation and Rounding – Primary 5 Mathematics Worksheets with Answers (NERDC)
standard_text: Round whole numbers to the nearest ten, hundred, thousand and million; estimate sums, differences, products and quotients; use the number line. (summary of the NERDC Primary 5 Mathematics curriculum)
meta_desc: Free Primary 5 maths worksheets on rounding to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000, estimating answers and checking with estimates. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Look at the next digit: 5 or more, round up
body_html:
How to think about it

  • To round, look at the digit to the right of the place you are rounding to. If it is 5 or more, round up; if it is 4 or less, round down.
  • Estimate by rounding each number first: 4,867 + 3,214 ≈ 5,000 + 3,000 = 8,000.
  • On a number line, a rounded number is the nearest marked number.

Examples

Example

Round 647,382 to the nearest 10,000

Next digit 7 → round up

Answer: 650,000

Example

Estimate 49 × 31

50 × 30

Answer: 1,500

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Looking at the wrong digitLook only at the digit just to the right.
Changing the digits after the rounding place to other numbersThey all become zeros.
Thinking an estimate must be exactAn estimate is close, not exact.

faq.a: To check that an answer is sensible.

faq.q: What is 35 rounded to the nearest ten?

faq.a: No. ≈ means is about equal to.

items.q: Estimate the value of 38 × 52 by rounding each number to the nearest ten.
items.e: 38 ≈ 40 and 52 ≈ 50. 40 × 50 = 2,000. (4 × 5 = 20, then write 2 zeros.) (1,500 rounds 38 down to 30, but 38 is nearer to 40.)

items.q: Estimate the value of 69 × 21 by rounding each number to the nearest ten.
Estimate the value of 618 ÷ 19 by rounding 618 to the nearest hundred and 19 to the nearest ten.
items.e: 618 ≈ 600 and 19 ≈ 20. 20 = 2 × 10, so divide by 10 first, then by 2. 600 ÷ 10 = 60, and 60 ÷ 2 = 30. (60 divides by 10, not by 20.)

items.q: Estimate the value of 412 × 29 by rounding 412 to the nearest hundred and 29 to the nearest ten.
Which is the best estimate for 79 × 32?
items.e: Round each number to the nearest ten: 79 ≈ 80 and 32 ≈ 30. So 80 × 30 = 2,400. The exact answer, 2,528, is close to 2,400.

Which is the best estimate for 4,830 ÷ 59?
items.e: Round 4,830 to the nearest hundred (4,800) and 59 to the nearest ten (60). 4,800 ÷ 60 = 480 ÷ 6 = 80.

Kayode works out 52 × 39 = 2,028. Which estimate shows that his answer is reasonable?
items.e: Round to the nearest ten: 52 ≈ 50 and 39 ≈ 40. 5 × 4 = 20, then write 2 zeros: 50 × 40 = 2,000. 2,028 is close to 2,000, so it is reasonable.

c: About 300, so it is not reasonable
About 3,000, so it is not reasonable
items.e: 61 ≈ 60 and 48 ≈ 50. 60 × 50 = 3,000. 29 280 is about 10 times too big, so Ali’s answer is not reasonable. (The exact answer is 2,928.)

items.q: Uche works out 38,460 + 24,915 and gets 53,375. Round each number to the nearest 1,000 to estimate the answer. What is the estimate?
items.e: 38,460 rounds to 38,000 and 24,915 rounds to 25,000. 38,000 + 25,000 = 63,000. (The exact answer is 63,375, so the estimate is close.) Uche’s answer is too far from 63,000, so it must be wrong.

items.q: A newspaper says “about 60,000 fans” were at a concert. The number was rounded to the nearest 10,000. Which could be the real number?
items.e: Numbers from 55,000 to 64,999 round to 60,000. 56,200 is in that range. 54,800 rounds down to 50,000, and 65,000 and 66,300 round up to 70,000.

items.q: About 400,000 people live in a city, rounded to the nearest 100,000. What is the greatest number of people who could live there?
items.e: Numbers from 350,000 to 449,999 round to 400,000. 450,000 rounds up to 500,000, so the greatest is 449,999.

items.q: A poster says the Moon is about 400,000 km away. The real distance is 384,400 km. What was it rounded to?
items.e: To the nearest 100,000, 384,400 rounds up to 400,000. To the nearest 10,000 it is 380,000, and to the nearest 1,000 it is 384,000.
